domain_name: Internal control frameworks and SOX scope
source: Original KaiSip notes written from the public law: the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, SEC rules, releases and staff guidance, and the public summaries published by COSO and the AICPA, all opened 31 Oct 2026. Not affiliated with or endorsed by SOXCPA. COSO framework text is not reproduced; principles are named only. COSO is a trademark of the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission.
overview: This domain covers the yardsticks companies use to judge internal control and what falls inside a Section 404 assessment. It starts with COSO's internal control framework, the 1992 original and the 2013 update, contrasts it with COSO's enterprise risk management frameworks of 2004 and 2017, and ends with scope: software, spreadsheets and outsourced service organizations.
analogy: Think of a building inspection. The building code is the framework: owner and inspector measure against it, and a new edition replaces the old one. A wider city plan covers zoning and growth, much as ERM covers strategy and enterprise risk, but the inspection still uses the code. Everything that holds the building up gets inspected, whether bought ready-made, built on site or maintained by a contractor, and hiring a contractor never moves the owner's duty to pass inspection.

topics.overview: COSO's 1992 framework gave U.S. companies a shared definition of internal control and the five components still used today. The SEC accepted it as a suitable yardstick for management's Section 404 evaluation, so its vocabulary runs through every ICFR report.
can_do: Define internal control the COSO way and explain why assurance is only reasonable
Name the 1992 objective categories and the five components without mixing up the cube's faces
Explain what SEC rules require of management's framework, and where COSO fits
Decide whether a safeguarding or compliance control falls inside the SEC's ICFR

subtopics.name: Internal Control as a Process
subtopics.definition: Internal control, in COSO's definition, is a process carried out by the board, management and other personnel to give reasonable assurance that objectives will be achieved.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Every Section 404 report rests on this idea. Seeing internal control as a people-driven process with reasonable, not absolute, assurance stops you treating a policy binder or one department as the whole control system.
how_it_works: It is a process: ongoing tasks and activities, a means to an end rather than a document or a department.
It is carried out by people at every level, not just written into manuals, systems and forms.
It gives reasonable assurance, never absolute: judgment can be faulty, people make errors, and management can override controls or staff can collude (COSO 2013 Executive Summary).
The 2013 update kept this core definition from 1992, so both editions agree on it (COSO 2013 FAQ, Question 1).
The SEC's ICFR definition in Rule 13a-15(f) keeps the reasonable-assurance idea, narrowed to reliable financial reporting.
subtopics.example: At a regional airline, the new treasurer finds a thick controls manual and assumes the control work is done. The finance director explains that the manual only describes controls; what counts is whether staff actually perform the reconciliations and approvals each month. The treasurer then plans checks of the people performing those controls, not just a read of the manual.

review: Compare documented controls with what staff actually perform each period
Trace management's effectiveness claim to evidence of controls operating
evidence: Signed reconciliations and approvals showing who performed each control
Management's ICFR assessment memo stating the framework and conclusion
audit_focus.recommend: Have management treat internal control as an operating process and support its assessment with evidence of performance.
audit_focus.decides: Management concludes on effectiveness; the board oversees internal control

subtopics.isaca_rule: Internal control is a process run by people that gives reasonable, not absolute, assurance. A manual, a department or an auditor's test is not the control system itself.

exam_traps.trap: Effective internal control guarantees that objectives will be met.
exam_traps.why: COSO limits it to reasonable assurance: faulty judgment, simple errors, management override and collusion can defeat even a well-designed system.

exam_traps.trap: Internal control is the internal audit department's job.
exam_traps.why: The board, management and other personnel all effect internal control. Internal audit is one role among many, and SOX does not itself require an internal audit function.

key_terms.definition: A high but not absolute level of confidence; internal control can never rule out every failure.
Managers bypassing controls they are meant to follow, one of the limits on any system of internal control.

subtopics.memory_aid: Process, people, reasonable: internal control is never a binder and never a guarantee.

subtopics.name: Objectives, Components and the Cube
subtopics.definition: The 1992 framework links three objective categories (operations, financial reporting, compliance) to five components, drawn as a cube with the entity's units as the third face.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Exam items swap the cube's faces. Knowing which list holds objectives, which holds components and which holds the entity's structure lets you reject an option that calls a component an objective or borrows ERM's categories.
how_it_works: Objectives (1992): effective and efficient operations, reliable financial reporting, and compliance with laws and regulations (SEC Release No. 33-8238, describing COSO 1992).
Components: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring.
Cube: objectives on one face, components on another, and the entity's units or activities on the third (COSO 2013 Executive Summary keeps the cube).
The SEC's ICFR is only the financial reporting slice, plus compliance with laws tied directly to preparing financial statements (Release No. 33-8238).

rows.label: What it lists
cells: Control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, monitoring
The entity, its divisions, operating units and functions

subtopics.example: A logistics company's compliance lead reviews a training slide on COSO. The draft lists monitoring as an objective and compliance as a component. The lead moves monitoring to the component row, keeps compliance with operations and financial reporting as objectives, and labels the third face with the company's divisions before the slide goes out.

review: Compare management's framework mapping with COSO's components and objectives
Trace each key control to a component and a financial reporting objective
evidence: Control matrix mapping each key control to a COSO component
Scoping memo naming the objectives and units in scope
audit_focus.recommend: Have the SOX program lead map each key control to a COSO component and the financial reporting objective.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides how its controls map to the framework

subtopics.isaca_rule: Keep the cube's faces apart: three objectives (1992: operations, financial reporting, compliance), five components, and the entity's structure. For SOX, ICFR is the financial reporting slice.

exam_traps.trap: Monitoring is one of COSO's objective categories.
exam_traps.why: Monitoring is a component. The objectives are operations, financial reporting (widened to all reporting in 2013) and compliance.

exam_traps.trap: The 1992 framework had four objective categories, including strategic.
exam_traps.why: Strategic objectives belong to COSO's 2004 ERM framework. The internal control framework has three categories.

key_terms.definition: COSO's picture linking objectives, components and the entity's organizational structure as three faces of one cube.
The SEC's term for the financial reporting part of internal control, defined in Rule 13a-15(f).

subtopics.memory_aid: Objectives: what you aim for. Components: what you need. Units: where it happens.

subtopics.name: COSO as a Suitable Framework
subtopics.definition: SEC rules require management to evaluate ICFR against a suitable, recognized framework set through due process; the SEC accepted COSO as one such framework without mandating it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Management's report must name its framework. Knowing that COSO is accepted but not compulsory, and why a home-made checklist fails the test, answers the framework-choice questions.
how_it_works: Rule 13a-15(c): the framework must be suitable and recognized, set by a body that followed due process, including broad distribution for public comment.
Release No. 33-8238 (2003): COSO satisfies the SEC's criteria, but the SEC does not mandate any framework, since others exist or may be developed.
Item 308(a)(2) of Regulation S-K: management's annual report must state which framework it used.
The SEC's 2007 guidance (Release No. 33-8810) explains one way to evaluate ICFR; it does not replace the framework.
subtopics.example: A software company's new chief accounting officer wants to swap COSO for a checklist the officer's team wrote over a weekend. The general counsel notes that the rule needs a recognized framework built through public due process and named in the annual report. The officer keeps COSO and uses the team's checklist only as an internal testing aid.

review: Confirm the framework named in management's report is suitable and recognized
Compare the framework named in the report with the one actually used
evidence: Management's annual ICFR report showing the framework statement
Audit committee minutes reviewing the assessment approach
audit_focus.recommend: Have management name the framework it used and keep internal checklists as testing aids only.
audit_focus.decides: Management selects the framework; SEC rules set the suitability test

subtopics.isaca_rule: Rule 13a-15(c): a suitable, recognized framework from a due-process body. COSO qualifies, but the SEC does not require it. Item 308(a)(2): the report names the framework used.

exam_traps.trap: SEC rules require every issuer to use the COSO framework.
exam_traps.why: Release No. 33-8238 says COSO satisfies the SEC's criteria but does not mandate it; another suitable, recognized framework is allowed.

exam_traps.trap: Management may use any internal checklist it designs as its framework.
exam_traps.why: Rule 13a-15(c) requires a recognized framework from a body that followed due process, including broad distribution for public comment.

key_terms.definition: Developing a framework openly, including wide distribution for public comment, as Rule 13a-15(c) requires.
The SEC's 2007 interpretive guidance on how management can evaluate ICFR using a top-down, risk-based approach.

subtopics.memory_aid: Suitable, recognized, due process: COSO passes, but it is not compulsory.

subtopics.name: What the SEC's ICFR Takes from COSO
subtopics.definition: The SEC's internal control over financial reporting takes COSO's financial reporting slice, adds safeguarding of assets that could materially affect the statements, and leaves out operations objectives.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Scope decides what management tests and reports under Section 404. A control can matter to the business yet sit outside ICFR, or move inside it when the financial statements come to depend on it.
how_it_works: Rule 13a-15(f) defines ICFR around reliable financial reporting and lists three kinds of policies: records, recording and authorization, and safeguarding of assets.
Clause (3) covers preventing or promptly detecting unauthorized acquisition, use or disposition of assets that could materially affect the financial statements.
The SEC wrote safeguarding in to follow COSO's 1994 addendum, because COSO 1992 placed safeguarding mainly under operations (SEC Release No. 33-8238, Section II.A.3).
Left out: COSO's operations objectives, and compliance objectives other than laws directly related to preparing the financial statements, such as the SEC's reporting rules (same release).
A warehouse fence is normally an operations control, but it supports financial reporting when interim figures rely solely on perpetual inventory records (Release No. 33-8238, footnote 57).
subtopics.example: A parking operator collects cash at unattended kiosks and records revenue from the kiosk counts. The controller keeps kiosk key custody and count segregation in ICFR scope, since cash taken before counting would understate revenue, and leaves a customer wait-time target out of the ICFR assessment.

review: Compare the ICFR scope memo with the three clauses of Rule 13a-15(f)
Test whether asset-protection controls are scoped where statements rely on records
evidence: Scoping memo explaining why each control is in or out of ICFR
Process map showing how interim inventory figures are produced
audit_focus.recommend: Have the SOX lead write down the ICFR scope reason for each asset-protection and compliance control.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides the ICFR scope under the SEC's definition

subtopics.isaca_rule: ICFR is COSO's financial reporting slice plus safeguarding of assets that could materially affect the statements. Operations controls, and compliance controls unrelated to preparing the statements, stay outside unless the statements come to depend on them.

exam_traps.trap: Safeguarding of assets is an operations objective, so it is never part of ICFR.
exam_traps.why: Rule 13a-15(f)(3) puts safeguarding in ICFR where unauthorized acquisition, use or disposition of assets could materially affect the financial statements.

exam_traps.trap: ICFR covers every compliance control, because COSO has a compliance objective.
exam_traps.why: The SEC's definition keeps only compliance with laws directly related to preparing the financial statements, such as the SEC's own reporting rules.

key_terms.definition: Controls that prevent or promptly detect unauthorized acquisition, use or disposition of a company's assets.
Running records that update inventory quantities with each receipt and sale between physical counts.

subtopics.memory_aid: Reporting slice plus asset guarding; operations and unrelated compliance stay out.

topics.overview: COSO updated the framework in May 2013 and treated the 1992 edition as superseded after 15 December 2014. The update kept the definition and the five components, set out 17 principles, widened the reporting objective and spelled out when internal control is effective.
can_do: Explain what the 2013 update kept, added and widened
Place a described activity under the right component and principle
Apply the present, functioning and operating-together test to a scenario
Explain why SEC filers classify deficiencies with SEC terms, not COSO's

subtopics.name: What Changed in 2013
subtopics.definition: COSO's 2013 update kept the 1992 definition and five components, set out 17 principles, and widened financial reporting into reporting of all kinds.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Items test what changed and what did not. A learner who thinks 2013 added a component, or that 1992 is still current, picks the wrong answer and may describe the framework wrongly in a filing.
how_it_works: Kept: the core definition, the five components and the need for each to be present and functioning (COSO 2013 FAQ, Question 1).
Added: 17 principles that formalize concepts already in the 1992 text, with points of focus as supporting characteristics (FAQ, Questions 1 and 4).
Widened: reporting now covers internal and external, financial and non-financial reporting (COSO 2013 Executive Summary).
Superseded: COSO treated the 1992 framework as superseded after 15 December 2014 and asked external reports to say which edition was used (FAQ, Question 6).
SOX assertions: COSO expected no change to management's 404(a) and the auditor's 404(b) assertions (FAQ, Question 5).
Points of focus help judge a principle; COSO does not require each to be assessed separately, and some may not suit every entity (FAQ, Question 4).
subtopics.example: In 2014 a consumer-goods company's SOX team still documented controls against the 1992 text. Before the deadline, the controller compares each control with the 17 principles, finds two principles with no supporting controls, assigns owners to close them, and changes the annual report wording to name the 2013 edition.

review: Compare the control matrix with all 17 principles for gaps
Confirm the annual report names the edition of COSO used
evidence: Principle-by-principle mapping of key controls with named owners
Annual ICFR report text naming the 2013 framework
audit_focus.recommend: Have the SOX program lead keep a dated gap log per principle and update the report's framework citation.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides the framework edition and owns any gaps

subtopics.isaca_rule: 2013 kept the definition and the five components, made 17 principles explicit and widened reporting. The 1992 edition is history, superseded after 15 December 2014; name the edition you used.

exam_traps.trap: The 2013 update added a sixth component for technology.
exam_traps.why: There are still five components. Technology appears as a principle under control activities (general controls over technology), not as a component.

exam_traps.trap: Companies may keep reporting against the 1992 framework as the current edition.
exam_traps.why: COSO considered the 1992 framework superseded after 15 December 2014 and asked external reports to state which edition was used.

key_terms.definition: Important characteristics of a principle; they help assess it but need not be assessed separately.
An edition replaced by a newer one; COSO treats the 1992 framework as superseded after 15 December 2014.

subtopics.memory_aid: Same definition, same five components, seventeen principles, wider reporting.

subtopics.name: The 17 Principles
subtopics.definition: The 17 principles are fundamental concepts under five components: five in control environment, four in risk assessment, three in control activities, three in information and communication, two in monitoring.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Placing an activity under the right component and principle is a common item type. It also shows management where its control set has gaps, because every relevant principle must be present and functioning.
how_it_works: Control environment (1 to 5): integrity and ethics, board independence and oversight, structures and authority, competent people, accountability (COSO 2013 Executive Summary).
Risk assessment (6 to 9): clear objectives, identifying and analyzing risks, considering the potential for fraud, assessing significant changes.
Control activities (10 to 12): selecting control activities, general controls over technology, and deploying them through policies and procedures.
Information and communication (13 to 15): quality information, internal communication and external communication.
Monitoring activities (16 and 17): ongoing or separate evaluations, and reporting deficiencies in time to those who must act.
subtopics.example: A hospital group adds a new billing system mid-year. The risk lead records the change under risk assessment's principle on significant changes, the IT lead maps access and change controls to general controls over technology, and the controller sends a deficiency found in testing to the CFO and the audit committee under monitoring.

review: Trace each principle to at least one supporting control
Inspect principles with no mapped control as possible gaps
evidence: Principle-to-control mapping approved by the SOX program lead
Deficiency log showing the principle each gap affects
audit_focus.recommend: Have process owners add or document controls for any principle with no supporting control.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides, rarely, that a principle is not relevant

subtopics.isaca_rule: Name the component, then the principle: five, four, three, three, two. Fraud risk sits in risk assessment; general controls over technology sit in control activities; deficiency reporting sits in monitoring.

exam_traps.trap: Considering fraud risk is part of the control environment.
exam_traps.why: Considering the potential for fraud is risk assessment principle 8. The control environment covers integrity, oversight, structure, competence and accountability.

exam_traps.trap: General controls over technology form their own component.
exam_traps.why: They are principle 11 under control activities; the five components did not change in 2013.

key_terms.definition: Risk assessment principle: the organization considers the potential for fraud when assessing risks to its objectives.
Control activities principle: the organization selects and develops general control activities over technology.

subtopics.memory_aid: Five, four, three, three, two: seventeen principles across five components.

subtopics.name: When Internal Control Is Effective
subtopics.definition: Under COSO 2013, internal control is effective when each component and relevant principle is present and functioning and the five components operate together as one system.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Present means designed and in place; functioning means it keeps working in practice. A documented control nobody performs fails the test, and SEC filers must also apply the SEC's deficiency terms.
how_it_works: Present: the component or principle exists in the design and implementation of the system (COSO 2013 Executive Summary).
Functioning: it continues to exist in the operation and conduct of the system.
If a relevant principle is not present and functioning, its component cannot be present and functioning (COSO 2013 FAQ, Question 3).
Operating together: the five components work as one integrated system that, taken together, keeps the risk of missing an objective acceptably low (COSO 2013 Executive Summary).
SEC filers classify severity only with SEC terms: control deficiency, significant deficiency, material weakness (FAQ, Question 3).
A material weakness at year-end means management cannot conclude ICFR is effective (Item 308(a)(3)).
subtopics.example: A shipping company's purchasing policy requires two approvals above a set limit, but a quarter's sample shows single approvals throughout. The internal control lead records the principle as present but not functioning, rates the deficiency with the CFO using the SEC's severity definitions, and reports it to the audit committee.

review: Compare documented design with evidence the control operated during the period
Evaluate deficiencies across components using the SEC's severity definitions
evidence: Test results showing each key control operated through the period
Deficiency evaluation memo classifying severity in SEC terms
audit_focus.recommend: Have management classify each deficiency with SEC definitions and disclose any material weakness in its annual report.
audit_focus.decides: Management concludes on effectiveness; the audit committee oversees

subtopics.isaca_rule: Effective means present, functioning and operating together. A relevant principle that fails pulls its component down. For SOX, use the SEC's deficiency terms; a material weakness at year-end means ICFR is not effective.

exam_traps.trap: A control documented in policy counts as present and functioning.
exam_traps.why: Documentation shows presence at most. Functioning needs evidence that the control actually operated during the period.

exam_traps.trap: COSO's 'major deficiency' label decides severity in a Section 404 report.
exam_traps.why: COSO says that where regulators set criteria, as the SEC does, management uses only those criteria to classify severity.

key_terms.definition: COSO's test: the component or principle exists in the design and keeps operating in practice.
COSO's term for a deficiency that stops an entity concluding its internal control is effective.

subtopics.memory_aid: Present on paper, functioning in practice, operating together as one.

subtopics.name: Applying the Framework to Cyber Risk
subtopics.definition: COSO's 2015 paper COSO in the Cyber Age shows how the 2013 internal control framework's five components and 17 principles can be used to manage cyber risk.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Cyber attacks can disrupt systems that process transactions and hold data. Using the familiar components gives boards, management and IT staff one shared language for cyber risk and its controls.
how_it_works: Commissioned by COSO and written by Deloitte (January 2015), the paper applies the existing 2013 framework; it creates no new framework (COSO in the Cyber Age).
The cyber risk assessment begins by finding which information systems are most valuable, measured by their impact on the entity's objectives.
Principles 7 and 8 then guide analysis of likely attackers, their methods and fraud risk; principle 9 covers changes such as cloud use or outsourcing.
Trying to protect everything equally overprotects some systems and underprotects others (same paper).
Control activities layer preventive and detective controls, including general controls over technology (principle 11).
Control environment and monitoring are foundational: if they are not present and functioning, cyber controls are unlikely to work.
subtopics.example: A regional hospital applies COSO to cyber risk: it first rates which systems matter most to billing and reporting, then studies who would attack those and how, then layers access, logging and review controls.

review: Compare the cyber risk assessment with the ranking of critical systems
Trace each critical system to its preventive and detective controls
evidence: Systems inventory with business impact ratings
Threat profile prepared for the most critical systems
audit_focus.recommend: Have the risk team agree system rankings with business owners before cyber control selection.
audit_focus.decides: Management sets cyber risk priorities under board oversight

subtopics.isaca_rule: Cyber risk uses the same five components and 17 principles. Begin with the information systems most critical to objectives, then the threats to them, then layered controls; never try to protect everything equally.

exam_traps.trap: A cyber risk assessment should start by listing threat actors and their attack methods.
exam_traps.why: COSO's 2015 paper starts with which information systems are most valuable to the entity's objectives; threat analysis then focuses on those systems.

exam_traps.trap: COSO created a separate cyber framework with its own components.
exam_traps.why: COSO in the Cyber Age applies the existing 2013 framework's components and principles to cyber risk.

key_terms.definition: Identifying and analyzing cyber threats to the information systems that matter most to an entity's objectives.
Several preventive and detective controls placed so that intruders who pass one defense still meet others.

subtopics.memory_aid: Crown jewels first, attackers second, layered controls third.

topics.topic_name: ERM (2004) and how it differs from internal control
topics.overview: COSO's 2004 Enterprise Risk Management—Integrated Framework built a broader model around internal control: eight components, a strategic objective category and its own cube. It helps manage risk across the enterprise, but Section 404 asks for an assessment of internal control over financial reporting.
can_do: List the eight 2004 ERM components and spot the ones internal control lacks
Name the four ERM objective categories
Explain why ERM is broader than internal control and does not replace the Section 404 assessment
Tell risk appetite from risk tolerance and name the four 2004 response options

subtopics.name: The 2004 ERM Components and Objectives
subtopics.definition: COSO's 2004 ERM framework has eight interrelated components and four objective categories, adding a strategic category to operations, reporting and compliance.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Distractors mix the 2004 ERM lists with the internal control lists. Knowing which components ERM adds, such as event identification, lets you spot the swap quickly.
how_it_works: Eight components: internal environment, objective setting, event identification, risk assessment, risk response, control activities, information and communication, monitoring (COSO thought paper, 2011, Appendix A).
Four objective categories: strategic, operations, reporting and compliance (COSO risk appetite thought paper, 2012).
Its cube sets objectives and components against the entity's levels, from entity-level to subsidiary.
Beyond internal control's five, ERM adds objective setting, event identification and risk response, and opens with the internal environment.
Internal control has no objective-setting component: objectives are a precondition to risk assessment, under principle 6 (COSO 2013 Executive Summary).

rows.label: Components only in ERM
cells: Objective setting, event identification, risk response

subtopics.example: A chemicals maker's new risk committee asks its chief risk officer to start an ERM program. The officer first agrees strategic objectives with management, then runs workshops on events that could help or hurt them, and records a chosen response for each. The SOX team keeps its separate internal control assessment for the annual report.

review: Sample the risk register for entries lacking a named owner
Trace each significant risk to a recorded risk response
evidence: Risk register showing identified events and chosen responses
Committee minutes approving strategic objectives and risk appetite
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief risk officer file workshop outputs and the chosen treatment for every major exposure.
audit_focus.decides: Management chooses risk responses; the board oversees risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: ERM 2004: eight components and four objective categories. Objective setting, event identification and risk response are ERM additions; strategic is the extra objective category.

exam_traps.trap: COSO's 2004 ERM framework has five components, like internal control.
exam_traps.why: The 2004 ERM framework has eight. Five components belong to internal control, and the 2017 ERM update also has five, but different ones.

exam_traps.trap: Strategic objectives are one of internal control's objective categories.
exam_traps.why: Strategic is ERM's fourth category. Internal control has operations, reporting and compliance.

key_terms.definition: ERM 2004 component: identifying events, risks or opportunities, that could affect achieving objectives.
ERM 2004 component: choosing whether to accept, reduce, share or avoid a risk.

subtopics.memory_aid: ERM 2004: eight components, four objectives, strategic first.

subtopics.name: ERM Versus Internal Control for SOX
subtopics.definition: ERM is broader than internal control and includes it; Section 404 requires management's report on internal control over financial reporting, not an ERM program.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A common trap says ERM replaced the internal control framework for SOX, or that SOX requires ERM. Both are wrong, and believing either leads to the wrong framework in an annual report.
how_it_works: Enterprise risk management is broader in scope than internal control, and internal control is an integral part of it (COSO 2013 FAQ, Question 8).
The two frameworks are complementary, and neither supersedes the other (COSO 2013 Executive Summary, foreword).
Statutes and rules may not require ERM, while regulators do require entities to maintain and report on effective internal control (FAQ, Question 8).
Section 404(a) and Item 308(a) require management's report on internal control over financial reporting, evaluated against a suitable framework.
subtopics.example: At a media group, a director proposes skipping this year's SOX testing because the new ERM program covers all risks. The CFO explains that ERM supports strategy, but the annual report still needs management's assessment of ICFR against its control framework, so testing goes ahead on schedule.

review: Read the scoping memo to confirm SOX testing is not replaced by ERM
Confirm the annual report names an internal control framework
evidence: Signed Form 10-K page carrying management's assessment
ERM charter describing its strategy and enterprise risk scope
audit_focus.recommend: Have the CFO record in the SOX plan why ERM work supplements, not substitutes for, ICFR testing.
audit_focus.decides: Management chooses the frameworks; the board oversees both

subtopics.isaca_rule: ERM is broader and includes internal control; neither framework supersedes the other. Section 404 asks for management's assessment of ICFR, so ERM does not replace the internal control assessment.

exam_traps.trap: COSO ERM replaced the internal control framework for Section 404 purposes.
exam_traps.why: COSO says the two are complementary and neither supersedes the other, and Section 404 calls for an assessment of internal control over financial reporting.

exam_traps.trap: SOX requires large companies to run an ERM program.
exam_traps.why: COSO notes entities may not be required by statute or rules to apply ERM. Section 404 requires reporting on ICFR.

key_terms.definition: COSO's broader framework for managing risk across the entity; internal control is an integral part of it.
Frameworks used side by side for different purposes, where neither replaces the other.

subtopics.memory_aid: ERM contains internal control; it does not replace it.

subtopics.name: Risk Appetite, Tolerance and Responses (2004)
subtopics.definition: In COSO's 2004 ERM framework, risk appetite is the broad amount of risk an entity accepts in pursuit of value; risk tolerance applies it to specific objectives.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Appetite sets the outer limit for strategy, and tolerances tell operating units how much variation is acceptable. Mixing them up leaves staff without usable limits, and responses then lack a yardstick.
how_it_works: Risk appetite: the amount of risk, on a broad level, an entity is willing to accept in pursuit of value (COSO risk appetite thought paper, 2012, quoting the 2004 framework).
Risk tolerance: the acceptable variation around a specific objective, best measured in that objective's own units (same paper, page 11).
Appetite is broad and strategic; tolerance is tactical and operational, and staying within tolerances keeps the entity within appetite.
Risk assessment follows event identification and comes before risk response (COSO thought paper Risk Assessment in Practice, 2012).
Risk response examines four options, accept, reduce, share or avoid, weighs costs and benefits and chooses a response (same paper).
subtopics.example: A water utility's board states a low appetite for service-disruption risk. Management sets tolerances of no more than four outage hours per customer a year and capital projects within 5% of budget, then records its choice to share drought risk through a supply agreement.

review: Compare stated risk tolerances with the board's risk appetite statement
Trace each major risk to a recorded response choice
evidence: Appetite statement recorded in board minutes
Risk register showing the response chosen for each major risk
audit_focus.recommend: Have management express tolerances in each objective's own measures and record the response chosen for every major risk.
audit_focus.decides: Directors own the appetite; operating management owns tolerances

subtopics.isaca_rule: Appetite is the broad limit set with strategy; tolerance is the measurable band around one objective. After assessing a risk, ERM 2004 responds by accepting, reducing, sharing or avoiding it.

exam_traps.trap: Risk tolerance is the board's overall statement of how much risk the entity accepts.
exam_traps.why: That is risk appetite. Tolerance applies appetite to a specific objective, as acceptable variation measured in that objective's units.

exam_traps.trap: Choosing to accept, reduce, share or avoid a risk is part of risk assessment.
exam_traps.why: In ERM 2004 those choices make up the risk response component, which comes after risk assessment.

key_terms.definition: The acceptable level of variation around a specific objective, usually measured in the same units as that objective.
Accept, reduce, share or avoid: the four ways ERM 2004 lets an entity respond to an assessed risk.

subtopics.memory_aid: Appetite is the whole plate; tolerance is each portion.

topics.overview: In 2017 COSO updated its ERM framework as Enterprise Risk Management—Integrating with Strategy and Performance. It reorganized ERM into five components and 20 principles and moved risk into choosing a strategy, not only carrying it out.
can_do: Name the five 2017 ERM components and tell them from the internal control components
Explain how the 2017 framework uses risk when a strategy is chosen
Reject the claim that ERM 2017 updated the internal control framework
Place risk appetite and the portfolio view in their 2017 components

subtopics.name: Five Components and 20 Principles
subtopics.definition: COSO's 2017 ERM framework is a set of 20 principles grouped into five components, from governance and culture to information, communication and reporting.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The 2017 numbers sit beside internal control's 17 principles and the 2004 ERM's eight components, so items swap them. The 2017 component names also differ from internal control's five.
how_it_works: Components: governance and culture; strategy and objective-setting; performance; review and revision; information, communication and reporting (COSO ERM 2017 Executive Summary).
Twenty principles sit under those components, for example defining risk appetite and developing a portfolio view.
ERM 2017 updates the 2004 ERM framework; it is not an update of the internal control framework.
COSO stresses that ERM is not a function or department, not just a risk list and not a checklist.
subtopics.example: A water utility's board asks its risk officer to modernize a program built on the 2004 model. The officer regroups its activities under the five 2017 components, adds a risk appetite the board approves, and starts reporting a portfolio view of risk each quarter, while the SOX team's internal control work stays as it is.

review: Map each existing ERM activity to its 2017 component and principle
Confirm the board approved a defined risk appetite
evidence: Signed appetite statement with the board approval date
Quarterly aggregated exposure report sent to directors
audit_focus.recommend: Have the risk officer keep a mapping table from old activities to the 2017 principles and file it for directors.
audit_focus.decides: The board concurs with risk appetite; management runs ERM

subtopics.isaca_rule: ERM 2017: five components, 20 principles, risk tied to strategy and performance. Do not confuse it with internal control's five components and 17 principles, or with ERM 2004's eight components.

exam_traps.trap: COSO's 2017 ERM publication updated the internal control framework.
exam_traps.why: It updated the 2004 ERM framework. The internal control framework was updated separately in 2013.

exam_traps.trap: ERM 2017 keeps the 2004 cube and its eight components.
exam_traps.why: The 2017 framework reorganized ERM into five components supported by 20 principles.

key_terms.definition: The types and amount of risk an organization is willing to accept in pursuit of value.
Looking at the amount of risk taken across the whole entity, not one risk or unit at a time.

subtopics.memory_aid: Internal control 17, ERM 2017 20: count the principles, not the components.

subtopics.name: Risk in Strategy Selection
subtopics.definition: ERM 2017 asks boards and management to weigh risk when choosing a strategy: whether it fits the mission and values, what risk profile it brings, and what threatens it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The update's main shift is from managing risks to a strategy already chosen toward using risk to choose the strategy. Items test whether you notice the two aspects a narrow risk review leaves out.
how_it_works: Risks to the chosen strategy: what could stop the strategy from working.
Strategy not aligning: a strategy that does not support the mission, vision and core values can fail the mission even if carried out well.
Implications from the strategy: each alternative has its own risk profile, weighed against risk appetite.
The board reviews, challenges and concurs with management on proposed strategy and risk appetite (COSO ERM 2017 Executive Summary).
subtopics.example: A ferry operator's management proposes moving into air freight. Before deciding, the board asks how air freight fits a mission built on regional passenger service and what risk profile it carries against the stated appetite. Management returns with a comparison of the options, and the board challenges its assumptions before voting.

review: Compare strategy papers with the risk appetite the board approved
Inspect each option paper for a separate exposure analysis
evidence: Board papers comparing alternative strategies and their risk profiles
Minutes showing the board challenged strategy and appetite
audit_focus.recommend: Have management attach an exposure comparison and a values check to every option paper sent to directors.
audit_focus.decides: Directors approve the chosen direction after challenging management

subtopics.isaca_rule: ERM 2017 looks at three things: risks to the chosen strategy, whether the strategy fits the mission and values, and the risk profile of each alternative. Risk shapes the choice, not only the execution.

exam_traps.trap: ERM only needs to list the risks to a strategy after it is chosen.
exam_traps.why: COSO 2017 adds two aspects that can affect value more: the strategy not aligning with mission and vision, and the implications of the strategy chosen.

exam_traps.trap: ERM is complete once every risk is listed in an inventory.
exam_traps.why: COSO says ERM is more than a risk listing; it includes the practices management uses to manage risk actively.

key_terms.definition: The possibility that a chosen strategy does not support the organization's mission, vision and core values.
The risk profile that comes with each alternative strategy, weighed against risk appetite before choosing.

subtopics.memory_aid: Fit, profile, threats: three questions before and after choosing a strategy.

subtopics.name: Risk Appetite and the Portfolio View (2017)
subtopics.definition: In COSO's 2017 ERM framework, risk appetite is defined while setting strategy, and the performance component builds a portfolio view of the total risk the entity takes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Business units can each stay within their own limits while their combined risk breaches what the board accepted. Setting appetite with strategy and checking a portfolio view closes that gap.
how_it_works: Strategy and objective-setting holds principle 7, defines risk appetite in the context of creating, preserving and realizing value (COSO ERM 2017 Executive Summary).
The same component analyzes business context, evaluates alternative strategies and formulates business objectives (principles 6, 8 and 9).
Performance identifies risk, assesses severity, prioritizes against appetite, implements responses and develops a portfolio view (principles 10 to 14).
Governance and culture holds board risk oversight (principle 1); review and revision assesses substantial change (principle 15).
subtopics.example: An airline's fuel, currency and route teams each report their own risk measures. The chief risk officer combines them into one view of total earnings at risk and compares it with the board's appetite.

review: Compare the entity-wide risk profile with the board's risk appetite
Trace how business-line exposures are combined into one view
evidence: Portfolio report aggregating exposures across business lines
Board minutes reviewing strategy and risk appetite together
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief risk officer combine exposures across units and report them against appetite to the board.
audit_focus.decides: Management proposes appetite with strategy; the board reviews and concurs

subtopics.isaca_rule: Appetite is set with strategy (strategy and objective-setting, principle 7); the portfolio view of total risk sits in performance (principle 14). Units within their own limits do not prove the whole is within appetite.

exam_traps.trap: Risk appetite is defined under governance and culture, because the board oversees risk.
exam_traps.why: Board oversight is principle 1 in governance and culture, but ERM 2017 places defining risk appetite in strategy and objective-setting, principle 7.

exam_traps.trap: If every unit stays within its own limits, the entity is within its risk appetite.
exam_traps.why: Only a portfolio view of combined exposure, principle 14 in performance, shows whether the total fits the board's appetite.

key_terms.definition: The ERM 2017 component where business context is analyzed, risk appetite defined, strategies evaluated and objectives set.
The ERM 2017 component that identifies, assesses and prioritizes risks, selects responses and builds the portfolio view.

subtopics.memory_aid: Appetite with strategy; portfolio in performance.

topics.overview: SOX scope follows financial reporting risk, not the type of tool. Purchased software, in-house systems and spreadsheets are in scope when a control that addresses a financial reporting risk depends on them, and so are the IT general controls those controls rely on.
can_do: Decide whether a system or spreadsheet is in scope from the risk it supports
Name the IT general control areas and evaluate only the ones that matter
Pick the control that protects a spreadsheet's access, formulas or changes
Explain which of several controls management may select and how IT fits the top-down approach

subtopics.name: Which Systems Are in Scope
subtopics.definition: A system or tool is in SOX scope when a control that addresses a financial reporting risk depends on it, whether it was purchased, built in-house or is a spreadsheet.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Scoping too narrowly leaves material risks untested; scoping too widely wastes effort. The SEC's top-down approach ties scope to financial reporting risk, not to how software was acquired.
how_it_works: Start top-down: identify financial reporting risks, then the controls that address them (SEC Release No. 33-8810, Section II.A.1).
Controls may be automated, depend on IT functionality such as a formula, or be manual steps using system reports (Release No. 33-8810).
When a control depends on IT, management considers the application control and the IT general controls behind it.
Rule 13a-15(f) defines ICFR by what it achieves for financial reporting, not by the technology used.
subtopics.example: An engineering firm's SOX lead reviews two tools: the enterprise system module that calculates depreciation on equipment, and a staff cafeteria ordering app. The lead scopes in the depreciation module and the general controls supporting it, leaves the cafeteria app out because it addresses no financial reporting risk, and records the reasoning in the scoping memo.

review: Trace each significant account to the systems its key controls use
Inspect excluded systems for any link to financial reporting risk
evidence: Scoping memo linking accounts, risks, controls and systems
System inventory showing which applications support key controls
audit_focus.recommend: Have the SOX lead scope systems by financial reporting risk and document why any system is excluded.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides SOX scope from its risk assessment

subtopics.isaca_rule: Scope follows the risk: if a control that addresses a financial reporting risk depends on a system or spreadsheet, it is in scope, however the tool was bought or built.

exam_traps.trap: Off-the-shelf software is outside SOX scope because the vendor tested it.
exam_traps.why: Scope depends on whether controls that address financial reporting risks rely on the software, not on who wrote it.

exam_traps.trap: Every system the company runs must be tested for SOX.
exam_traps.why: The SEC's top-down, risk-based approach brings in only the systems that support controls addressing financial reporting risks.

key_terms.definition: Starting from financial reporting risks and working down to the controls and systems that address them.
An automated control inside a system, such as matching, error checking or edit checking.

subtopics.memory_aid: Follow the risk, not the vendor.

subtopics.name: IT General Controls
subtopics.definition: IT general controls are controls over the IT environment, such as program development, program changes, computer operations and access, that keep automated controls working consistently.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Automated controls are only as reliable as the general controls around them. The SEC limits the required evaluation to the general controls that matter for financial reporting, which keeps the assessment focused.
how_it_works: Example areas: program development, program changes, computer operations, and access to programs and data (SEC Release No. 33-8810, Section II.A.1.d).
Management evaluates only the general controls needed for other controls that address financial reporting risks to operate properly and consistently.
General controls alone ordinarily do not address financial reporting risks; they support the application controls that do.
General controls that mainly serve operational efficiency need not be evaluated for ICFR.
COSO 2013 principle 11 covers selecting and developing general control activities over technology.
Combination controls, such as a person investigating items on a computer-generated exception report, bring both the manual step and the IT behind the report into scope (footnote 36).
subtopics.example: A credit union's automated interest calculation is a key control. The IT compliance lead tests change management on the core banking system, because an unapproved code change could alter the calculation, but leaves the help desk's response-time targets out of the SOX plan because they affect efficiency, not financial reporting.

review: Trace each automated key control to the general controls it relies on
Inspect change and access records for in-scope applications
evidence: Change tickets with approvals and test results for in-scope applications
User access reviews for systems supporting key controls
audit_focus.recommend: Have IT management test the general controls that support key automated controls and document each link.
audit_focus.decides: IT and finance management agree which supporting controls matter

subtopics.isaca_rule: Evaluate the IT general controls that keep in-scope automated controls working, not every IT control. General controls support application controls; alone they rarely address a financial reporting risk.

exam_traps.trap: Management must test every IT general control in all four example areas.
exam_traps.why: The SEC lists the areas as examples; management evaluates only the general controls needed for controls that address financial reporting risks.

exam_traps.trap: Strong IT general controls alone show that a financial reporting risk is addressed.
exam_traps.why: The SEC says general controls alone ordinarily do not address financial reporting risks; the application or manual controls they support do.

key_terms.definition: Controls over the IT environment, such as change, access and operations, that support consistent automated controls.
The general control area covering approval and testing of changes to programs before they go live.

subtopics.memory_aid: General controls hold up the application controls; test the ones that carry weight.

subtopics.name: Spreadsheet Controls
subtopics.definition: Spreadsheet controls protect calculations that feed the financial statements: who can open and edit the file, how formula changes are approved, and how inputs and results are checked.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Spreadsheets often carry estimates and allocations into the ledger with little IT oversight. A changed formula or a wrong input can misstate results while the file still looks fine.
how_it_works: Release No. 33-8810 (footnote 35) gives consistent application of a formula as IT functionality a control can depend on; a key spreadsheet formula fits that, and the ICFR definition.
Access: limit who can open and edit the file and its inputs.
Change and version control: approve and record each formula change, and keep the approved version.
Input and formula checks: agree inputs to source records and test formulas against the intended logic.
Review: check the logic as well as the result, and keep evidence for management's assessment (Item 308, Instruction 2).
subtopics.example: A pharmaceutical company accrues customer rebates in a spreadsheet each quarter. The controller locks the formula cells, keeps the approved version in a controlled folder, has a second accountant agree the inputs to the rebate contracts, and logs each formula change with its approval before the quarter's numbers are posted.

review: Compare the spreadsheet in use with the last approved version
Reperform key formulas and trace inputs to source records
evidence: Change log showing approved formula changes with dates
Reviewer sign-off noting the logic and inputs checked
audit_focus.recommend: Have the spreadsheet owner lock formulas, approve and log changes, and evidence the review of logic.
audit_focus.decides: The process owner designs the spreadsheet's controls

subtopics.isaca_rule: A spreadsheet is in scope when a key control depends on it. Protect it like a small system: limited access, approved and logged changes, input and formula checks, and a review of logic as well as totals.

exam_traps.trap: A spreadsheet is in scope only if IT registers it as a system of record.
exam_traps.why: Scope follows the financial reporting risk. If a key control depends on the spreadsheet's calculation, it is in scope however it is labeled.

exam_traps.trap: A reviewer checking the final total controls the spreadsheet's formulas.
exam_traps.why: A total can look reasonable with a broken formula. Formula changes need approval and logging, and the review should cover the logic.

key_terms.definition: Tools such as spreadsheets that business users build and run outside formal IT development.
Keeping an approved version of a file and recording each change, who made it and who approved it.

subtopics.memory_aid: Lock it, log it, check it, review the logic.

subtopics.name: Automated Controls in Management's Evaluation
subtopics.definition: When several controls each address a financial reporting risk, management may evaluate the one it can test most efficiently, and automated controls often qualify when IT general controls work.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Testing every control that touches a risk wastes effort. The SEC's guidance lets management focus on controls that adequately address the risk and are efficient to evaluate, with IT scoped inside the same approach.
how_it_works: Where more than one control adequately addresses a risk, management may select the one whose operating evidence is obtained more efficiently (SEC Release No. 33-8810, Section II.A.1.b).
With effective IT general controls, automated controls may be more efficient to evaluate than manual ones (same section).
Automated controls on a stable system with effective IT general controls may be assessed as lower risk than judgmental manual controls (Release No. 33-8810, Section II.A.2.a).
Identifying IT risks and controls is part of the top-down, risk-based approach, not a separate evaluation (Release No. 33-8810, Section II.A.1.d).
subtopics.example: A utility's billing risk is covered both by an automated rate-table check in its billing system and by a supervisor's monthly sample review of bills. General controls over the billing system tested effective, so management evaluates the automated check as its key control and notes why it adequately addresses the risk.

review: Compare each risk's selected key control with the documented rationale
Inspect IT general control results before relying on automated controls
evidence: Risk and control matrix naming one key control per risk
IT general control test results for systems behind automated controls
audit_focus.recommend: Have the SOX lead justify each key control choice against the risk and the evidence it needs.
audit_focus.decides: Management chooses which controls support its assessment

subtopics.isaca_rule: Evaluate controls that adequately address the risk, choosing the most efficient to evaluate when several do. Effective IT general controls make automated controls efficient to rely on, and IT is scoped inside the top-down approach.

exam_traps.trap: Management must test every control that addresses a financial reporting risk.
exam_traps.why: Release No. 33-8810 lets management select, among controls that each adequately address the risk, the one whose evidence it can evaluate most efficiently.

exam_traps.trap: IT risks are scoped in a separate IT review after the business processes.
exam_traps.why: The SEC says identifying IT risks and controls should be an integral part of the top-down, risk-based approach, not a separate evaluation.

key_terms.definition: A control performed by software each time, such as an automated three-way match, without a person acting.
A control management selects and evaluates because it adequately addresses a financial reporting risk.

subtopics.memory_aid: Several good controls? Test the efficient one; IT rides along top-down.

topics.topic_name: Service organizations: from SAS 70 to SSAE 18
topics.overview: Companies outsource processes that feed their financial statements, but they keep responsibility for ICFR. A service auditor's SOC 1 report, formerly a SAS 70 report, gives evidence about the provider's controls; management still controls what flows to and from the provider.
can_do: Explain who stays responsible for ICFR when a process is outsourced
Tell a Type 1 report from a Type 2 report and pick the one a scenario needs
Decide what management reports when it cannot get evidence from a service organization
Trace the service auditor standard from SAS 70 to SSAE No. 18 and tell it from the user auditor's

subtopics.name: Outsourcing Keeps the Responsibility
subtopics.definition: When a company outsources a process that affects its financial statements, its own management stays responsible for assessing the controls over that process for Section 404.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Outsourcing moves the work, not the accountability. Management's annual report covers the whole of ICFR, outsourced processes included, so management needs evidence that those controls work.
how_it_works: Management keeps the responsibility to assess controls over outsourced operations (SEC staff ICFR FAQ, revised 24 Sept. 2007, Question 8).
Management may rely on a service auditor's Type 2 report, even one as of a different year-end.
The staff said management cannot rely on such a report if management engaged its own audit firm to prepare it.
Management stays responsible for controls over information flowing to and from the service organization.
subtopics.example: A wholesale distributor moves freight invoicing to an outside processor. The controller obtains the processor's Type 2 report, maps its controls to the distributor's invoicing risks, and keeps in-house checks that the files sent to the processor and the results returned are complete and accurate.

review: Trace each outsourced process to the evidence management relied on
Inspect controls over data sent to and received from the provider
evidence: Service auditor's Type 2 report mapped to the company's risks
Reconciliations of data exchanged with the service organization
audit_focus.recommend: Have management obtain evidence on the provider's controls and keep controls over data exchanged with it.
audit_focus.decides: User-company management remains responsible for its ICFR

subtopics.isaca_rule: Outsourcing a process never outsources SOX responsibility. The user company's management assesses the controls, may rely on a Type 2 report, and keeps controls over what goes to and comes back from the provider.

exam_traps.trap: Once a process is outsourced, the service organization answers for its controls under Section 404.
exam_traps.why: The SEC staff says the user company's management keeps the responsibility to assess controls over outsourced operations.

exam_traps.trap: A service auditor's report covers everything management needs for the outsourced process.
exam_traps.why: Management still owns the controls over information flowing to and from the service organization.

key_terms.definition: A company that uses a service organization for processing that affects its own financial statements.
An outside provider whose services, such as processing transactions, affect a user entity's financial reporting.

subtopics.memory_aid: Outsource the work, keep the duty.

subtopics.name: Type 1 and Type 2 Reports
subtopics.definition: A Type 2 service auditor's report adds tests of whether controls operated effectively over a period; a Type 1 report speaks as of a date, without those tests.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Management needs evidence that outsourced controls worked during the year. Only a Type 2 report tests operating effectiveness, and SOC 1 is the report aimed at user entities' financial reporting.
how_it_works: Type 2: controls described, suitably designed, placed in operation, and tested for operating effectiveness during a period (SEC staff ICFR FAQ, footnote 3; Release No. 33-8810, footnote 54).
Type 1: speaks as of a date, without the tests of operating effectiveness over a period that define a Type 2 report.
SOC 1 examines a service organization's controls likely to be relevant to user entities' ICFR (AICPA SOC 1 page).
SOC 1 reports were formerly known as SAS 70 reports; service auditors now examine under SSAE No. 18 (AICPA).
SOC 2 reports address trust services criteria such as security and availability, not ICFR (AICPA SOC suite page).

rows.label: Covers
cells: Controls as of a date, without operating-effectiveness tests
Controls plus tests of operating effectiveness

subtopics.example: A medical device maker stores finished goods at an outside warehouse. The controller receives a Type 1 report and notes it has no tests of operating effectiveness. The controller asks for the warehouse's Type 2 report covering most of the fiscal year and plans the company's own testing of receiving controls for the months it does not cover.

review: Match the service auditor's test window to the company's year-end
Inspect the report type, scope and any exceptions found
evidence: SOC 1 Type 2 report with its period, opinion and test results
Workpapers for in-house tests of the gap period
audit_focus.recommend: Have management obtain a SOC 1 Type 2 report and test any months it does not cover.
audit_focus.decides: User-company management decides whether the evidence is enough

subtopics.isaca_rule: Need proof that outsourced controls worked? A SOC 1 Type 2 report over a period. A Type 1 speaks as of a date without operating tests; SOC 2 addresses trust services criteria, not ICFR.

exam_traps.trap: A Type 1 report shows that controls operated effectively.
exam_traps.why: Only a Type 2 report includes tests of operating effectiveness over a period (SEC staff ICFR FAQ, footnote 3); a Type 1 report has no such tests.

exam_traps.trap: A SOC 2 report is the right evidence for a Section 404 assessment.
exam_traps.why: SOC 1 addresses controls relevant to user entities' ICFR; SOC 2 reports on trust services criteria such as security and availability.

key_terms.definition: An examination of a service organization's controls likely to be relevant to user entities' ICFR.
The older auditing standard whose service auditor reports are now known as SOC 1 reports.
The AICPA attestation standard under which service auditors now examine and report on service organization controls.

subtopics.memory_aid: Type 1 is a snapshot; Type 2 adds a period of tested proof.

subtopics.name: When No Evidence Is Available
subtopics.definition: If management cannot get evidence about an outsourced process, it cannot report a scope limitation; it must judge whether the gap means ICFR is not effective.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A provider may refuse to share a report or allow access. Management's report must still say whether ICFR is effective, so the gap has to be judged, not carved out.
how_it_works: Item 308(a)(3): management's report states whether ICFR is effective, and any material weakness rules out an effective conclusion.
The rules do not allow a management ICFR report with a scope limitation (SEC Release No. 33-8810, Section II.B.5).
First look for alternatives: a Type 2 report, direct access to test, or compensating controls in-house.
Without them, management judges whether the inability to assess is significant enough to conclude ICFR is not effective.
One staff allowance: a newly acquired business may be excluded, with disclosure, for up to one year from acquisition (SEC staff ICFR FAQ, Question 3).
subtopics.example: A specialty insurer's reinsurance accounting runs through a broker that refuses any report or testing access. The chief accounting officer adds detailed in-house recalculations of the broker's statements as a compensating control, tests them through year-end, and documents why that evidence supports the conclusion in management's report.

review: Confirm management sought a Type 2 report or direct access
Evaluate compensating controls covering the outsourced process
evidence: Correspondence showing the request and the provider's refusal
Recalculation workpapers signed by the reviewer at each quarter-end
audit_focus.recommend: Have management build and test compensating controls, or judge whether the gap makes ICFR ineffective.
audit_focus.decides: Management concludes on effectiveness without a scope limitation

subtopics.isaca_rule: No scope limitations in management's ICFR report, beyond the staff's one-year allowance for a newly acquired business. If outsourced evidence is out of reach and nothing compensates, management judges whether ICFR is not effective.

exam_traps.trap: Management may leave out an outsourced process it cannot assess and call it a scope limitation.
exam_traps.why: The SEC says its rules do not permit a scope limitation; the staff allows only a newly acquired business to be excluded, for up to one year.

exam_traps.trap: The independent auditor's 404(b) attestation covers what management could not assess.
exam_traps.why: Section 404(b) attests to management's assessment; it does not replace management's own evaluation under Section 404(a).

key_terms.definition: Leaving part of ICFR out of the conclusion; not permitted in management's annual ICFR report.
A control that addresses the same risk when another control is missing or cannot be assessed.

subtopics.memory_aid: Can't see it? Judge it; never carve it out.

subtopics.name: From SAS 70 to SSAE 18
subtopics.definition: Service auditor reports have moved from SAS 70 reports to SOC 1 reports, which service auditors now issue under SSAE No. 18, the AICPA's recodified attestation standards.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The SEC's 2007 staff answers still say 'Type 2 SAS 70 report'. Knowing the chain lets you read them as meaning today's SOC 1 Type 2 report.
how_it_works: SOC 1 reports were formerly known as SAS 70 reports (AICPA employee benefit plan SOC 1 resource page, opened 31 Oct 2026).
SSAE No. 18 recodified the attestation standards and superseded SSAE Nos. 10 to 17, SSAE No. 16 among them, except SSAE No. 15 (AICPA SSAE No. 18 page).
A SOC 1 examination falls under AT-C section 320, part of SSAE No. 18 as amended (AICPA SOC 1 guide page; AICPA list of SSAEs current as of August 2026).
The user auditor has a separate standard: user auditors of nonissuers follow AU-C section 402; an issuer's auditor follows PCAOB standards (AICPA).
SOC 1 reports are intended for user entities and their auditors (AICPA SOC 1 page).
subtopics.example: A health insurer's controller finds the SEC staff's 2007 answer on 'Type 2 SAS 70 reports' and asks what to request from its claims processor today. The SOX lead requests a SOC 1 Type 2 report issued under SSAE No. 18 for the fiscal-year period and maps it to the insurer's claims risks.

review: Inspect the standard named in each SOC 1 report's opinion
Map report periods and control objectives to the company's risks
evidence: Service auditor's opinion page stating standard and period
Mapping of report control objectives to financial reporting risks
audit_focus.recommend: Have management request current SOC 1 Type 2 reports and read older 'SAS 70' guidance as referring to them.
audit_focus.decides: User-company management decides whether a report is enough evidence

subtopics.isaca_rule: Read 'SAS 70 report' in older SEC guidance as today's SOC 1 report. Service auditors examine under SSAE No. 18 (AT-C section 320); user auditors of nonissuers follow AU-C section 402, and an issuer's auditor follows PCAOB standards.

exam_traps.trap: SSAE No. 16 is still the current standard for SOC 1 examinations.
exam_traps.why: SSAE No. 18 recodified and superseded SSAE Nos. 10 to 17 (except No. 15), so SOC 1 examinations now fall under AT-C section 320.

exam_traps.trap: AU-C section 402 governs the service auditor's SOC 1 examination.
exam_traps.why: It guides a nonissuer's auditor whose client uses a service organization; issuer audits follow PCAOB standards. Service auditors use SSAE No. 18.

key_terms.definition: The AICPA attestation section, within SSAE No. 18 as amended, under which a service auditor performs a SOC 1 examination.
The AICPA auditing section for a nonissuer's auditor whose client uses a service organization; issuer audits follow PCAOB standards.

subtopics.memory_aid: Service auditor: AT-C 320. Nonissuer's user auditor: AU-C 402. SAS 70 is the old name.

key_terminologies.COSO: The Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission, which publishes the internal control and ERM frameworks.
key_terminologies.Internal control: A process effected by the board, management and other personnel that gives reasonable assurance about operations, reporting and compliance objectives.
key_terminologies.Reasonable assurance: High but not absolute confidence; no system of internal control can rule out every failure.
key_terminologies.Five components: Control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring activities.
key_terminologies.17 principles: The fundamental concepts COSO 2013 set out under the five components; relevant ones must be present and functioning.
key_terminologies.Present and functioning: Exists in the design of the system and keeps operating in practice.
key_terminologies.Suitable framework: A recognized control framework set by a body that followed due process, as Rule 13a-15(c) requires.
key_terminologies.ICFR: Internal control over financial reporting, the SEC's financial reporting slice of internal control (Rule 13a-15(f)).
key_terminologies.Enterprise risk management (ERM): COSO's broader framework for managing risk across the entity, which includes internal control.
key_terminologies.Event identification: An ERM 2004 component: finding events that could affect objectives, as risks or opportunities.
key_terminologies.Risk appetite: The types and amount of risk an organization is willing to accept in pursuit of value.
key_terminologies.Top-down, risk-based approach: The SEC's 2007 method: start from financial reporting risks, then find the controls and systems that address them.
key_terminologies.IT general controls: Controls over program development, program changes, computer operations and access that support automated controls.
key_terminologies.Application control: An automated control inside a system, such as matching or edit checks.
key_terminologies.End-user computing: Spreadsheets and similar tools built and run by business users outside formal IT development.
key_terminologies.Service organization: An outside provider whose services affect a user entity's financial reporting.
key_terminologies.SOC 1 report: A service auditor's report on controls likely to be relevant to user entities' ICFR; formerly a SAS 70 report.
key_terminologies.Type 1 report: A service auditor's report as of a date, without the tests of operating effectiveness that a Type 2 report adds.
key_terminologies.Type 2 report: A service auditor's report that adds tests of operating effectiveness over a specified period.
key_terminologies.Scope limitation: Leaving part of ICFR out of the conclusion; not allowed in management's annual ICFR report.
key_terminologies.Risk tolerance: The acceptable variation around a specific objective, measured in that objective's own units (ERM 2004).
key_terminologies.Safeguarding of assets: Preventing or promptly detecting unauthorized acquisition, use or disposition of assets; part of the SEC's ICFR definition where losses could materially affect the financial statements.
key_terminologies.SSAE No. 18: The AICPA's recodified attestation standards, under which service auditors now issue SOC 1 reports (AT-C section 320).
